title: 1. Lab Overview
text:
## 1. Lab Overview

This laboratory transforms a prepared TurtleBot 3 simulation model into a ROS2-enabled mobile robot. You will progressively add and validate the core capabilities needed for autonomous operation in simulation.

### At a glance

By the end of this lab, you will build a complete ROS2 mobile robot in Isaac Sim and verify that it can:

- publish simulation time on `/clock`
- receive velocity commands on `/cmd_vel`
- drive using differential-wheel control
- publish LIDAR data on `/scan`
- publish camera data on `/camera/image_raw`
- publish odometry and TF transforms
- localize the robot using AMCL and a saved map
- navigate to a goal using Nav2

The system is assembled incrementally, and each section ends with a validation checkpoint to confirm that the current stage is functioning correctly.

### Learning outcomes

After completing this laboratory, you will be able to:

- configure and validate real-time ROS2 communication in Isaac Sim
- build a differential-drive mobile robot controller
- publish sensor data from a simulated LIDAR and camera
- publish odometry and TF information for robot localization
- configure AMCL and Nav2 for map-based navigation

> Important: This lab is intentionally structured as a layered robotics integration exercise. Complete each section in order, and do not proceed until the current checkpoint is working.

text:
## How to Read an Isaac Sim Action Graph

> Node-name convention: In Isaac Sim 6.0.1, ROS bridge node names use `ROS2` without a space. For example, search for `ROS2 Context`, not `ROS 2 Context`. The surrounding explanation may continue to use the normal phrase “ROS 2.”

An Action Graph contains two different types of connections.

- Solid arrows carry data.
- Dashed arrows carry execution signals.

A node may have the correct data connection but still not operate if its execution input is not connected.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Tick["On Playback Tick"] -.->|"EXECUTION signal"| Publish["Publisher or Controller"]
    Context["ROS2 Context"] -->|"context handle"| Publish
    Data["Sensor or simulation data"] -->|"DATA"| Publish
    Time["Isaac Read Simulation Time"] -->|"timestamp"| Publish

```

Read every graph in this order:

1. Find the `On Playback Tick` node.
2. Follow the dashed execution arrows.
3. Find the `ROS2 Context` node.
4. Follow the context connection.
5. Follow the solid data arrows.
6. Check every node’s Property panel.
7. Press Play and validate the result in ROS2.

> Important: A graph is not complete when the nodes are merely present. A graph is complete only when the nodes, properties, and connections are correct.

> Visual rule: If an output port is connected, a visible wire must leave that port. If an input port is required, a visible wire must enter

that input port.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Tick["On Playback Tick"] -.->|"execIn"| Clock["ROS2 Publish Clock"]
    Time["Isaac Read Simulation Time"] -->|"timeStamp"| Clock
    Context["ROS2 Context"] -->|"context"| Clock
    Clock -->|"/clock"| ROS["ROS2 network"]

```

### Clock Graph: Required Port Connections

| Source node | Output port | Destination node | Input port | Connection type |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `On Playback Tick` | `tick` | `ROS2 Publish Clock` | `execIn` | Execution |
| `ROS2 Context` | `context` | `ROS2 Publish Clock` | `context` | Data |
| `Isaac Read Simulation Time` | `simulationTime` | `ROS2 Publish Clock` | `timeStamp` | Data |

The final graph must visually resemble:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Tick["On Playback Tick"] -.->|"1. execution"| Clock["ROS2 Publish Clock"]
    Context["ROS2 Context"] -->|"2. context"| Clock
    Time["Isaac Read Simulation Time"] -->|"3. timestamp"| Clock

```

> Stop and verify: Do not continue until the graph contains all three connections shown above.

BACK TO DASHBOARD
CHAPTER 01
THE SPARK OF LIFE! ⚡

Welcome to the world of robotics! Today, we're going to bring our first circuit to life. We'll learn how to make an LED blink using an Arduino. It's the "Hello World" of hardware!

title: Playbook: BASIC PRINCIPLES
text:
BASIC PRINCIPLES

Before we build, we need to understand the big three: Voltage, Current, and Resistance.

🔋
Voltage (V)
Think of it as the "push" or pressure that makes electricity flow. Measured in Volts.
🌊
Current (I)
The actual flow of tiny electrons moving through the wires. Measured in Amps.
🧱
Resistance (R)
Obstacles that slow down the current. Keeps things from blowing up! Measured in Ohms (Ω).

title: Playbook: LED
text:
LED

Light Emitting Diode. It glows when current passes through!

220Ω Resistor

Limits the flow of electricity so the LED doesn't pop.

Breadboard & Wires

For plugging things in without messy soldering.

🧮

title: Playbook: MATH & PHYSICS
text:
MATH & PHYSICS
V=IR
Ohm's Law

Ohm's Law is the most important formula in electronics. It connects Voltage, Current, and Resistance.

V = I × R

Voltage = Current × Resistance

Why a 220Ω Resistor?

Our Arduino supplies 5V. A typical red LED needs about 2V and likes a current of 0.02A (20mA).

R = (Supply Voltage - LED Voltage) / Current
R = (5V - 2V) / 0.02A
R = 3V / 0.02A
R = 150 Ohms

We use 220Ω because it's a common standard size and provides a safe buffer!

🔌

THE WIRING DIAGRAM

Follow these steps carefully!

Connect a jumper wire from Arduino GND to the negative (-) rail of the breadboard.
Place the LED on the breadboard. Note: The longer leg is Positive (Anode), the shorter is Negative (Cathode).
Connect the 220Ω Resistor from the negative (-) rail to the shorter leg of the LED.

CHAPTER 02
SENSE THE WORLD! 👁️

Time to give your robot a superpower — the ability to see! You'll build an automatic gate that opens when an object approaches and closes when it leaves. Along the way you'll learn how a robot reads an input, makes a decision, and controls an output.

LEARNING OBJECTIVES

2

title: Playbook: CORE CONCEPTS
text:
CORE CONCEPTS
🧠
Arduino Uno R3
The brain of the project. It runs your program, reads the IR sensor on a digital pin, and sends a control signal to the servo motor.
👁️
IR Sensor Module
Has an infrared LED and a receiver. When an object reflects infrared light back, the module changes its OUT signal. Most modules output LOW when an object is detected, but some output HIGH.
⚙️
Servo Motor (SG90)
A motor that can move to a chosen angle, usually 0° to 180°. It has three wires: power (red), ground (brown/black), and signal (orange/yellow).
🔀
Digital Input & Output
A digital pin reads or writes two states: HIGH or LOW. Pin 2 reads the sensor; Pin 9 sends the timed signal that controls the servo position.
⏚
Common Ground
All connected parts must share the same ground reference. Without it, the Arduino and modules may not agree on what HIGH and LOW mean, causing random behaviour.

title: Playbook: THE WIRING DIAGRAM
text:
THE WIRING DIAGRAM

Follow the connections carefully!

COMPONENT TERMINAL	→ ARDUINO PIN	WHAT IT DOES
IR Sensor VCC	5V	Provides power to the IR sensor
IR Sensor GND	GND	Completes the circuit, shares ground
IR Sensor OUT	Digital Pin 2	Sends HIGH/LOW reading to Arduino
Servo Red Wire	5V	Provides servo power (SG90)
Servo Brown/Black	GND	Servo ground — must connect to Arduino GND
Servo Orange/Yellow	Digital Pin 3	Receives the servo control signal

title: Playbook: IMPORTANT WIRING POINTS
text:
IMPORTANT WIRING POINTS
⏚
Common grounding is required — Arduino GND, IR sensor GND, and servo GND must all connect together.
🔍
Check terminals before powering: VCC → 5V, GND → GND, OUT/SIG → digital pin.
🚫
Do NOT connect VCC directly to GND. That creates a short circuit and can damage your board!
🔌
Small SG90 servos can run from Arduino 5V for a demo. Larger servos need a separate 5V supply.
🔗
If using a separate servo supply, connect supply negative to both servo GND and Arduino GND.
📌
Pin 9 is used for the servo signal because it supports PWM and is common in servo examples.
🔧
The IR sensor may have a small potentiometer screw — turning it adjusts detection distance.

IF
The Servo.h library is included so Arduino can control the servo easily.
IR sensor OUT → digital pin 2. Servo signal → digital pin 9.
In setup(), pin 2 is set as INPUT, the servo attaches to pin 9, and the gate starts closed (0°).
In loop(), Arduino reads the sensor value every cycle.
If an object is detected → servo moves to 90° (gate opens).
If no object → servo moves back to 0° (gate closes).
A small 50ms delay keeps readings stable.
🔬

Connect IR sensor GND → Arduino GND.
Connect IR sensor OUT → Arduino digital pin 2.
Connect servo red wire → Arduino 5V.
Connect servo brown/black wire → Arduino GND.
Connect servo orange/yellow wire → Arduino digital pin 9.
Attach the servo horn and optional cardboard gate arm.
Connect the Arduino to computer via USB.
Open Arduino IDE, paste the code, select Arduino Uno and the correct port, then upload.

title: Playbook: EXPECTED RESULT
text:
EXPECTED RESULT
🚧

When no object is in front of the IR sensor, the servo stays at 0° (gate closed).

When an object is detected, the servo turns to 90° for about one second (gate opens).

If the sensor behaves the opposite way, change objectDetectedState from LOW to HIGH in the code.

title: Playbook: TROUBLESHOOTING
text:
TROUBLESHOOTING
PROBLEM	LIKELY CAUSE	FIX
Servo does not move	Wrong power/ground/signal wire	Check red→5V, brown/black→GND, signal→pin 9
Sensor light changes but no servo reaction	OUT wire or code pin mismatch	Verify IR OUT goes to digital pin 2
Servo jitters or Arduino resets	Servo drawing too much current	Use separate 5V supply; connect grounds together
Servo moves opposite of expected	Sensor output logic is reversed	Change objectDetectedState from LOW to HIGH
Sensor detects too far or too near	Sensitivity needs adjustment	Turn the small potentiometer slowly and retest
Nothing works after wiring	No common ground or loose jumper	Reconnect all GND wires; press jumpers firmly

title: Playbook: SAFETY & GOOD PRACTICE
text:
SAFETY & GOOD PRACTICE
✅ Always check wiring before plugging in USB power.
✅ Keep metal objects away from exposed pins.
✅ Do not force the servo horn by hand while powered.
✅ Disconnect power before changing wires.
✅ Use colour coding: red for 5V, black/brown for GND, another colour for signal.

CHAPTER 03
MOVE IT! 🚗

Welcome to Chapter 3! Now that you've mastered the basics of electronics, it's time to build something that moves. In this chapter, we will build a smart, wireless-controlled car.

A Quick Note on Wireless Tech: Many beginner robotic cars use Bluetooth for local control. However, for this project, we are stepping into the world of IoT (Internet of Things)! We will use the ESP8266 NodeMCU microcontroller and the Blynk platform to control our car via WiFi. This means you can control your car from anywhere in the world, as long as both your phone and the car have internet access!

text:
THE PARTS LIST
ESP8266 NodeMCU

The brain of our car, featuring built-in WiFi capabilities.

L298N Motor Driver

Takes weak signals and uses them to switch high-power electricity to the motors.

DC Gear Motors

Convert electrical energy into mechanical movement.

🔋
Li-ion Batteries

Two 3.7V batteries in series (7.4V) to power the motors.

title: Playbook: POWER CONNECTIONS
text:
POWER CONNECTIONS
Connect the two Li-ion batteries in series (7.4V total).
Connect the Positive (Red) wire to the 12V terminal on the L298N.
Connect the Negative (Black) wire to the GND terminal on the L298N.
Connect a wire from the 5V terminal on the L298N to the Vin pin on the NodeMCU.
Connect another wire from the GND terminal on the L298N to a GND pin on the NodeMCU.

title: Playbook: MOTOR CONNECTIONS
text:
MOTOR CONNECTIONS
Motor 1 (Left): Connect to the OUT1 and OUT2 terminals.
Motor 2 (Right): Connect to the OUT3 and OUT4 terminals.
LOGIC CONNECTIONS (ESP8266 TO L298N)
ENA → D0
IN1 → D1
IN2 → D2
IN3 → D3
IN4 → D4
ENB → D5

How does it go in reverse?

The L298N uses an internal circuit called an H-Bridge. By changing the logic signals on IN1 and IN2 (e.g., from HIGH/LOW to LOW/HIGH), the H-Bridge flips the polarity of the electricity going to the motor, making it spin backward!

title: Playbook: SETTING UP BLYNK
text:
SETTING UP BLYNK

Blynk makes it easy to build apps that talk to microcontrollers over the internet using Virtual Pins.

STEP 1: WEB DASHBOARD
Create an account on the Blynk website.
Create a New Template named "WiFi control car" (Hardware: ESP8266).
Create three Virtual Pin datastreams:
X on pin V0 (0-100)
Y on pin V1 (0-100)
Speed on pin V2 (0-255)
Create a New Device from this template and save your BLYNK_AUTH_TOKEN.
STEP 2: MOBILE APP
Install the Blynk IoT app and log in.
Open your device and tap the setup icon.
Add a Slider and link it to Speed (V2).
Add a Joystick and link X to X (V0) and Y to Y (V1).
